title: JAPAN'S THANKSGIVING
subtitle: no turkey, all rice
source: Niinamesai / Niiname-no-Matsuri (earliest record in the Nihon Shoki, 673; emperor offers new rice to the kami and partakes of it); renamed Labor Thanksgiving Day (Kinro Kansha no Hi) in 1948; children's thank-you drawings for police, firefighters, hospital staff; KFC 'Kentucky for Christmas' since 1974

lines.say: [excited] Kon! Happy Thanksgiving! Where's the turkey?
[sly] Japan has a Thanksgiving too. No turkey.
[gasps] NO TURKEY?!
It's on November twenty-third. And it's about something way older than turkey. Rice.
The oldest record of it is from the year six seventy-three. It's called Niinamesai. The festival of new rice.
And shrines all over Japan still offer the year's new rice to the gods.
[hushed] On that night, the emperor offers the first rice of the harvest to the gods... and then eats it with them.
cap: offers the {o:first rice} of the harvest

lines.say: [hushed] It still happens every year, deep inside the palace, late into the night.
[impressed] So the gods get the first bite. Respect.
After World War Two, the holiday got a new name. Labor Thanksgiving Day.
cap: the holiday got a new name.

lines.say: Now it's about thanking the people who work hard for everyone else.
[warm] Kids draw thank-you cards for police officers, firefighters, and nurses.
Some kids walk their drawings right up to the little police box on their street.
[sweet] Aww. Okay, but what do people EAT?
[amused] Rice. Lots of rice.
[deflated] ...No turkey at all?
[sly] Japan saves the bird for Christmas. Fried chicken. Kentucky Fried Chicken.
[baffled] WHAT?!
Since nineteen seventy-four. Families order their buckets weeks ahead.
[amused] Christmas Eve is their busiest day of the whole year.
[warm] Okay. I'm thankful for rice, for firefighters... and for you, Kon.
[soft, sly] I'm thankful for your grandma's sushi.
[laughing] Kon!
